title: Feelings & opinions
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The person who FEELS something goes into the to-shape: мне холодно is literally "to me [it is] cold", with no subject at all and no verb. Saying it the English way — Я холодный — describes you as a cold sort of person, which is not what you meant. This to-shape is M1's мне, the third shape of я, finally doing the job it was listed for.

Liking runs backwards from English. In мне нравится Москва the thing liked is the SUBJECT and the verb agrees with IT: мне нравится книга (one thing) · мне нравятся книги (more than one). мне only names who is pleased and never changes. It is exactly M8's Сколько стоят книги? — a verb following the thing rather than the person.

потому что gives the REASON and поэтому gives the CONSEQUENCE. They map cleanly onto "because" and "so", which makes them one of the few free rides in the course — the same two facts, written in either order.
The comma is not optional. Russian writes one before потому что and one before что, always: Я думаю, что это хорошо. English drops both the comma and the word "that"; Russian drops neither.

Feelings that DO have a subject use M2's short predicate, which agrees with whoever is described: Я устал · Я устала. Keep the two shapes apart — мне холодно has no subject and cannot agree with anything, while я устал has one and must.

words.note: "Cold" — in the shape Russian uses when nothing in particular is being described, the same shape as M1's приятно. It describes the situation, not you, which is why the person feeling it goes into the to-shape in front of it.

sentences.trap: Я холодный is a real Russian sentence and it says that you are a cold person — unfeeling. The temperature version puts you in the to-shape and leaves the sentence without a subject at all.
sentences.sound: mnye KHO-lad-na. Three о letters in холодно and only the first is stressed; the other two flatten to "a".

variations.changed: мне → вам, the polite you in its to-shape — the third shape of вы, from M2
a name in its to-shape: Анна → Анне, the same ending as в комнате
не in front of what it denies — here the feeling, since there is no verb

mistake.why: The person feeling something goes into the to-shape: Мне холодно. Я холодно is not a sentence at all.

sentences.usage: Weather, rooms, and anything you feel rather than are — this frame covers a great many of them.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian does not say you are cold. It says that to you, it is cold.

words.note: "Hot", in the same shape as холодно and in the same frame. It is about temperature only — Russian does not use it the way English uses "hot" for anything else.

sentences.trap: The frame is worth more than the word. Once мне + a feeling-word is fixed, half a dozen everyday states come for free — and every one of them would be wrong with я.
sentences.sound: mnye ZHAR-ka. The ж is the s of English "measure", and the final о flattens as always.

variations.changed: the polite you in its to-shape — вам, from M2's row
не in front of the feeling word
M7's здесь instead of a person — the frame works about a place too, and still has no subject

mistake.why: That describes you as a hot object. The feeling is Мне жарко.

sentences.usage: Rooms, trains, summers — and complaining about them politely.
sentences.mnemonic: Cold, hot, dull, frightening: all of them happen TO you in Russian.

words.note: "Pleases". The thing liked is the SUBJECT, so the verb agrees with it — нравится for one thing, нравятся for more than one — and мне never changes, because it only names who is pleased. M1's люблю is the other way of liking: люблю is a stronger, more personal fondness, and нравится is closer to "I find it nice".

sentences.trap: Everything is the wrong way round from English. The city does the pleasing, you are the one pleased, and the verb answers to the city. Я нравлюсь Москве would say that Moscow likes YOU.
sentences.sound: mnye NRA-vee-tsa mask-VA. The -тся on the end is said "tsa", as one sound — the т and the с run together.

variations.changed: more than one thing, so the verb changes to нравятся — and мне does not
мне → вам: a different person is pleased, and нравится still follows Moscow
не in front of the verb — the same one word as ever

mistake.why: The person pleased goes into the to-shape: Мне нравится Москва. я is for the one doing something, and here that is the city.

sentences.usage: Opinions about places, films, food — and it is gentler than люблю, which is why it is the everyday choice.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not like it. It pleases you — and the verb agrees with it, not with you.

words.note: City, and also town — Russian does not split the two by size the way English does. Masculine, ending in a consonant, and here it is the SUBJECT of the sentence, so it is in its plain dictionary shape.

sentences.trap: город is not the object of anything, so it does not take M3's ending. In this frame the thing liked is always the subject and always keeps its dictionary shape.
sentences.sound: mnye NRA-vee-tsa GO-rat. The final д of город is said as a t, the way хлеб ends in a p.

variations.changed: a pointing word in front — этот agrees with what it points at
the polite you in its to-shape, asked rather than told
M1's verb instead — and now я is the subject and город is the object, the whole sentence turned round

mistake.why: города is a counting or plural shape. The thing liked is the subject, so it is город.

sentences.usage: Opinions about where you are — and the third variation is worth studying, because the two ways of liking build opposite sentences.
sentences.mnemonic: In this frame the thing liked is the subject, so it never bends.

words.note: "Why". Its answer is потому что, and the two look alike on purpose — почему asks and потому что replies. Nothing else in the question moves: no helper, no reordering.

sentences.trap: English needs "aren't" here — a helper carrying both the tense and the negation. Russian has не in front of the verb and a question mark at the end, and that is the entire machinery.
sentences.sound: pa-chee-MOO vy nye ra-BO-ta-ye-tye. The stress is right at the end of почему, and the pitch climbs after it.

variations.changed: a question with no verb at all — the zero copula, still running
a name instead of вы, and the verb takes the he/she ending
swap the verb — the frame takes any of them

mistake.why: не goes in front of the verb, not in front of the person. Почему вы не работаете?

sentences.usage: Asking for a reason — and its answer is the next two sentences.
sentences.mnemonic: почему asks; потому что answers. They rhyme because they are two halves of one exchange.

sentences.display: Я не работаю, потому что я устал.
sentences.cue: I am not working because I am tired
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I not work, because I got-tired"
sentences.literal: I not work, because I got-tired

words.note: "Because", in two words that are always written together and always preceded by a comma. It introduces the REASON, and the clause after it is an ordinary sentence with nothing rearranged.

sentences.trap: The comma before потому что is a rule, not a preference. Russian punctuation is much more tightly specified than English punctuation, and this is one of the places where leaving a comma out is simply an error.
sentences.sound: ya nye ra-BO-ta-yoo pa-ta-MOO shta ya oo-STAL. потому что runs together in speech and что is said "shta", not "chto".

variations.display: Я не работаю, потому что я устала.
variations.cue: I am not working because I am tired (said by a woman)
variations.changed: устал → устала: M2's rule, still following the speaker

variations.display: Я дома, потому что я устал.
variations.cue: I am at home because I am tired
variations.changed: swap the first half — потому что takes any statement on either side

variations.display: Я не работаю, потому что мне холодно.
variations.cue: I am not working because I am cold
variations.changed: a to-shape feeling as the reason — and it still has no subject

mistake.display: Я не работаю потому что я устал.
mistake.why: The comma is obligatory in Russian. It goes before потому что, every time.

sentences.usage: Explaining yourself — and the reason half is the longer, more useful half of the pair.
sentences.mnemonic: Comma, потому что, reason. The comma is part of the phrase.

sentences.display: Я устал, поэтому я не работаю.
sentences.cue: I am tired, so I am not working
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I got-tired, therefore I not work"
sentences.literal: I got-tired, therefore I not work

words.note: "So", introducing the CONSEQUENCE — the mirror image of потому что. Same comma rule, and the same two facts: put the reason first and use поэтому, or put it second and use потому что.

sentences.trap: The pair is easy and the choice is the lesson: which half of the sentence you write first decides which word you need. Getting them the wrong way round reverses cause and effect entirely.
sentences.sound: ya oo-STAL pa-E-ta-moo ya nye ra-BO-ta-yoo. поэтому is stressed on its second syllable, which is where the э is.

variations.display: Я устала, поэтому я не работаю.
variations.cue: I am tired, so I am not working (said by a woman)
variations.changed: устал → устала, following the speaker

variations.cue: I am cold, so I am at home
variations.changed: a to-shape feeling as the reason, and M5's дома as the consequence

variations.display: Я не работаю, потому что я устал.
variations.cue: I am not working because I am tired
variations.changed: the same two facts the other way round — so the word flips too

mistake.display: Я устал, потому что я не работаю.
mistake.why: That says you are tired BECAUSE you are not working — cause and effect swapped. With the reason first, the word is поэтому.

sentences.usage: Explaining a decision — and it is the more natural order in Russian conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: Reason first: поэтому. Reason second: потому что.

words.note: "I think", pattern I — думаю (I), думаете (you, polite), думает (he or she). It is for holding an opinion; Russian uses a different word for thinking about something in your head.

"That", joining an opinion to what it is about — and it can never be left out, where English drops "that" freely. The same word also means "what" as a question (Что это?), and the sentence tells you which. Said "shto" in the question and "shta" inside потому что.

sentences.trap: English can say "I think it's good" with no "that" and no comma. Russian requires both — the comma before что is as obligatory as the word itself.
sentences.sound: ya DOO-ma-yoo shto E-ta kha-ra-SHO. что is written with a ч and said with an sh, the same trick as конечно.

variations.changed: swap the opinion — the frame does not move

variations.cue: Do you think that is good?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, asked rather than told

variations.cue: I think Anna is at home
variations.changed: a whole statement after что, with the zero copula still running inside it

mistake.why: Two things missing that English can do without: the comma and что. Я думаю, что это хорошо.

sentences.usage: Any opinion, softened — and it is the politest way to disagree.
sentences.mnemonic: что and its comma both stay. English drops them; Russian never does.

words.note: "Bad" — the opposite of M2's хорошо, and it does the same two jobs: it answers Как дела? and it describes a verb (Я плохо говорю, "I speak badly"). In the to-shape frame it means feeling unwell rather than being a bad person.

sentences.trap: Мне плохо means you feel ill, not that things are going badly. For that, Russian answers Как дела? with плохо on its own — the same word without the мне.
sentences.sound: mnye PLO-kha. The х at the end is the raspy one, and the final о flattens to "a".

variations.changed: мне → вам — the question you would be asked if you looked pale
on its own, as the answer to Как дела? — and now it is about things, not about you
не in front of the feeling word

mistake.why: That says you are a bad person. Feeling unwell is Мне плохо.

sentences.usage: Saying you feel ill — and it is understood immediately as a request for help.
sentences.mnemonic: With мне it is about your body. Without it, it is about your day.

words.note: "I understand", pattern I — понимаю (I), понимаете (you, polite), понимает (he or she). The single most useful verb a beginner owns, and it is at its most useful with не in front of it.

sentences.trap: There is no do. "I don't understand" has a helper carrying the negation in English and Russian has none — не in front of the verb, and the sentence is finished, exactly as it was in M3.
sentences.sound: ya nye pa-nee-MA-yoo. Four syllables, the stress near the end, and every unstressed о flattened to "a".

variations.changed: drop не — and nothing else has to move back
the polite you-form, as a question

variations.display: Я не понимаю, потому что вы говорите быстро.
variations.cue: I don't understand because you speak fast
variations.changed: потому что joining the two halves — the module's frame doing real work

mistake.why: A dictionary shape cannot be the verb of its own sentence. It needs an ending: Я не понимаю.

sentences.usage: The most useful sentence in any language you are learning — and the third variation is how you ask for help without asking.
sentences.mnemonic: One word of negation, one verb with an ending. Russian never needs more than that.
